title: Advent: waiting
hookLine: four weeks of candles and longing before Christmas

cards: Think about the last time you really waited for something. A baby due any day. Test results.
A plane landing with someone you love on it. You can't make it come faster, and you can't stop looking at the door. Now picture an evergreen wreath on a kitchen table in December, with four candles.
On the first Sunday, one candle is lit. The next week, two. Then three.
Then four. Outside, the nights keep getting longer. Inside, the light slowly grows.

teach.b: Advent, from the Latin adventus: a coming, an arrival. It's the four Sundays before Christmas, and in Western churches it's where the church year begins. Advent looks two ways at once.

teach.h: BACK TO BETHLEHEM, FORWARD TO THE END.
teach.b: Back, to the first coming, the birth in Bethlehem, and the centuries of hoping before it. And forward, to what Christians call the second coming, when they believe Christ will return and set the world right.
So the readings are full of prophets. Isaiah: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light." John the Baptist in the desert, telling everyone to get ready.
The mood is purple: hope, with an ache in it. Many churches sing the old hymn O Come, O Come, Emmanuel, which sounds more like a plea than a party.

teach.h: A WREATH, ONE CANDLE A WEEK.
teach.b: The wreath is younger than people think. It's usually traced to a Lutheran pastor in nineteenth-century Germany who made a wheel of candles to help the children in his care count down the days.
Many wreaths now have three purple candles and one pink, for the third Sunday, when the mood turns toward joy; some add a white one in the middle for Christmas Day.
Orthodox Christians keep a longer season before Christmas, a forty-day fast.

And the whole thing ends with the Bible's own last prayer, in Revelation: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Advent says waiting isn't wasted time. For Christians it's a kind of prayer: keeping the door open, and the light on.

how: Many Christians keep Advent with a wreath of four candles lit one more each Sunday, with daily readings and quieter, expectant hymns; Orthodox Christians keep a forty-day Nativity fast before Christmas.

o: a season of waiting for Christ's coming
a feast for the first snowfall of winter

s: Advent is just a countdown to Christmas presents
it's a season of waiting and longing, looking back to Bethlehem and forward to Christ's return.
Advent looks forward to the second coming, not only back to the birth
it looks two ways at once.
the Advent wreath goes back to the first Christians

games.q: it's early December. the shops have played Christmas songs for weeks, but your church is still singing about waiting in the dark. why?
o: it's keeping Advent: longing before the feast.
games.why: Advent keeps the waiting on purpose. the celebrating starts on Christmas Day, and then it keeps going.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it; if not, turn on one small lamp or just picture a flame, then leave the phone alone and watch the light, noticing how hard it is to wait for nothing in particular.
If you pray, say the old line, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus," once, and wait some more. If you don't, let yourself notice what you're longing for.

wordCard.voice: Advent. From the Latin for coming. Four weeks of waiting and longing before Christmas, where the church year begins. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a coming, an arrival. once used for an emperor's visit to a city.

carryVoice: Your line: come, lord. Four candles, lit one week at a time. One hundred ten days, and counting.
